title: Harlem Awakens
p: In the decades after 1910, millions of African Americans left the rural South in what became known as the Great Migration, seeking jobs and escaping racial violence and segregation laws.
1910年以后的几十年里，数百万非裔美国人离开南方乡村，这就是后来所说的“大迁徙”，他们寻找工作，并逃离种族暴力和种族隔离法。
Many settled in Harlem, a neighborhood in upper Manhattan that by the 1920s had become the cultural capital of Black America.
许多人定居在曼哈顿北部的哈莱姆区，到20世纪20年代，那里已成为美国黑人的文化之都。
The flowering of art, literature and music that followed is called the Harlem Renaissance.
随之而来的艺术、文学和音乐的繁荣被称为“哈莱姆文艺复兴”。
Poets such as Langston Hughes wrote in the rhythms of jazz and blues, insisting that everyday Black life was a worthy subject for serious art.
兰斯顿·休斯等诗人以爵士乐和布鲁斯的节奏写诗，坚持认为黑人的日常生活是严肃艺术值得表现的题材。
Zora Neale Hurston, trained in anthropology, collected folk tales and later wrote novels that captured the speech of Southern Black communities.
受过人类学训练的佐拉·尼尔·赫斯顿收集民间故事，后来又写出了生动再现南方黑人社区语言的小说。
The era was full of contradictions.
这个时代充满了矛盾。
At the famous Cotton Club, Duke Ellington's orchestra performed for audiences from which Black customers were excluded.
在著名的棉花俱乐部，艾灵顿公爵的乐团为观众演出，而黑人顾客却被拒之门外。
Even so, the movement gave a generation a new sense of pride and laid cultural foundations for the civil rights struggles that came decades later.
即便如此，这场运动给了一代人新的自豪感，并为几十年后的民权斗争奠定了文化基础。
q: The movement of African Americans from the rural South
The move of jazz clubs to Chicago
A government program to build Harlem

It was a worthy subject for serious art
It should be kept out of poetry

title: The Golden Spike
p: On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in Utah, a ceremonial golden spike was tapped into place, joining two railroad lines and linking the eastern United States to the Pacific coast.
1869年5月10日，在犹他州的普罗蒙特里峰，一枚具有仪式意义的金色道钉被敲入轨道，将两条铁路连接起来，使美国东部与太平洋沿岸连通。
A telegraph operator sent a single word across the nation: "DONE."
一名电报员向全国发出了一个词：“完工”。
A journey that had taken months by wagon or ship could now be made in about a week.
过去乘马车或轮船需要数月的旅程，如今大约一周就能完成。
The Union Pacific had built westward from Nebraska, relying heavily on Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans.
联合太平洋铁路公司从内布拉斯加向西修建，主要依靠爱尔兰移民和南北战争退伍军人。
The Central Pacific, building east from Sacramento, faced the far harder task of crossing the Sierra Nevada, and it turned to Chinese workers, who eventually made up most of its labor force.
中央太平洋铁路公司从萨克拉门托向东修建，面临的是穿越内华达山脉这一艰巨得多的任务，于是它求助于华工，华工最终占了其劳动力的大部分。
They blasted tunnels through granite in brutal winters and were paid less than white workers, yet they were almost entirely absent from the famous photographs of the celebration.
他们在严酷的冬天炸穿花岗岩开凿隧道，工资却比白人工人低，然而在那些著名的庆典照片中几乎看不到他们的身影。
The railroad transformed the national economy, but it also accelerated the destruction of the great bison herds and the displacement of Native American nations.
这条铁路改变了美国经济，但也加速了大型野牛群的毁灭和美洲原住民部族的流离失所。
In recent years, historians and descendants have worked to restore the Chinese workers' place in the story.
近年来，历史学家和华工后裔一直在努力让华工在这段历史中重新获得应有的位置。
q: What happened at Promontory Summit on May 10, 1869?
Why was the Central Pacific's task harder?
It had to cross the Sierra Nevada
It started later than the Union Pacific

It had to cross the Mississippi River
What does the article say about the Chinese workers?

They were paid more than white workers
They built the Union Pacific line from Nebraska
They arrived after the railroad was finished

title: Two Versions of One Treaty
p: February 6 is Waitangi Day, New Zealand's national day, marking the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840 between representatives of the British Crown and more than 500 Māori chiefs.
2月6日是新西兰的国庆日怀唐伊日，纪念1840年英国王室代表与500多位毛利酋长签署《怀唐伊条约》。
The first signatures were added at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands, where ceremonial war canoes called waka still gather on the water each year.
最初的签名是在岛屿湾的怀唐伊签下的，每年仍有被称为“waka”的仪式战船在那里的水面上聚集。
Yet the treaty has long been a source of dispute, partly because its English and Māori versions do not say the same thing.
然而，这份条约长期以来一直是争议的源头，部分原因在于它的英文版和毛利文版内容并不一致。

In the English text, the chiefs cede "sovereignty" to Queen Victoria, while the Māori text uses kāwanatanga, a word closer to "governorship," and promises chiefs continued tino rangatiratanga, or full authority, over their lands and treasures.
英文本中，酋长们把“主权”让与维多利亚女王，而毛利文本使用的是“kāwanatanga”一词，更接近“治理权”，并承诺酋长们对其土地和珍宝继续拥有“tino rangatiratanga”，即完全的权威。
Most chiefs signed the Māori version, so many Māori understood they were sharing power, not surrendering it.
大多数酋长签署的是毛利文本，所以许多毛利人理解为他们是在分享权力，而不是交出权力。
In the decades that followed, large areas of Māori land were confiscated or sold under pressure.
此后的几十年里，大片毛利土地被没收或在压力下被出售。
Since 1975, a body called the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated claims of treaty breaches, leading to formal apologies and settlements.
自1975年起，一个名为怀唐伊特别法庭的机构开始调查违反条约的申诉，促成了正式道歉和和解赔偿。
As a result, Waitangi Day is both a celebration and a day of protest and reflection on what the nation's founding promise really meant.
因此，怀唐伊日既是庆祝的日子，也是抗议和反思的日子，人们思考这个国家的建国承诺究竟意味着什么。
q: The signing of a treaty in 1840
The arrival of the first Māori canoes
The end of a war in 1975
Why has the treaty caused disputes?
Its English and Māori versions differ
It was written only in French
It gave all land to the Māori
What does the Waitangi Tribunal do?

title: The Mountains Are Calling
p: John Muir was born in Scotland in 1838 and emigrated with his family to a Wisconsin farm as a boy, where his strict father made him work from dawn to dusk.
约翰·缪尔1838年生于苏格兰，童年时随家人移居威斯康星州的一个农场，严厉的父亲让他从早到晚地干活。
After an industrial accident nearly cost him his sight, he resolved to devote his life to studying nature, and in 1867 he set off on a walk of roughly 1,000 miles to the Gulf of Mexico.
一次工业事故几乎让他失明，此后他决心毕生致力于研究自然，并于1867年出发，步行约1000英里前往墨西哥湾。
The following year, he arrived in California and first saw Yosemite, a valley of sheer granite cliffs and thundering waterfalls in the Sierra Nevada.
第二年，他来到加利福尼亚，第一次见到了约塞米蒂——内华达山脉中一个满是陡峭花岗岩峭壁和轰鸣瀑布的山谷。
His essays, which blended scientific observation with almost religious wonder, persuaded many readers that wilderness deserved protection for its own sake.
他的文章将科学观察与近乎宗教般的赞叹融为一体，说服了许多读者：荒野本身就值得保护。

He helped campaign for Yosemite National Park, created in 1890, co-founded the Sierra Club in 1892, and in 1903 camped under the stars with President Theodore Roosevelt, urging him to protect more land.
他协助推动了1890年约塞米蒂国家公园的设立，1892年参与创办了塞拉俱乐部，并在1903年与西奥多·罗斯福总统一起露宿星空下，敦促他保护更多土地。
Not every battle was won.
并非每一场斗争都取得了胜利。
In 1913, despite Muir's fierce opposition, Congress approved a dam in Yosemite's Hetch Hetchy Valley to supply water to San Francisco, a defeat he felt deeply in the final year of his life.
1913年，尽管缪尔强烈反对，国会还是批准在约塞米蒂的赫奇赫奇山谷修建水坝，为旧金山供水，这场失败让他在人生的最后一年深感痛心。
Even so, he is often remembered as the "Father of the National Parks."
即便如此，他仍常被人们称为“国家公园之父”。

An accident that nearly cost him his sight
What did Muir do with President Roosevelt in 1903?
He camped with him and urged more protection
He sold him land in Yosemite
He argued for building a dam
He founded the Sierra Club with him
Why was the Hetch Hetchy decision a defeat for Muir?
A dam was approved there despite his opposition
